stem: The Vijayanagara Empire, whose capital is the subject of this chapter, was founded in the 14th century. Its name means the __________.
solution: The Vijayanagara Empire takes its name from its magnificent capital city, Vijayanagara — a Sanskrit name meaning the 'City of Victory' (vijaya = victory, nagara = city). The empire was founded in the 14th century (traditionally in 1336) in the Deccan/South India and became one of the most powerful states in southern India. The ruins of the capital are located at present-day Hampi in Karnataka. So Vijayanagara means the 'City of Victory'.

stem: The Vijayanagara Empire was founded around 1336 CE by two brothers, __________, who established the first ruling dynasty.
solution: According to tradition, the Vijayanagara Empire was founded around 1336 CE by two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, who established the first (Sangama) dynasty. The empire was ruled successively by four dynasties: the Sangama, the Saluva, the Tuluva (to which the famous Krishnadeva Raya belonged), and the Aravidu. So the founders were Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty.

stem: The ruins of the Vijayanagara capital are located at present-day __________, on the banks of the Tungabhadra river in Karnataka.
solution: The ruins of the Vijayanagara capital are located at Hampi (in the Bellary/Vijayanagara district of Karnataka), on the banks of the Tungabhadra river. The name 'Hampi' derives from Pampadevi (the local goddess/name of the Tungabhadra). The extensive and magnificent ruins at Hampi — temples, palaces, markets, and fortifications — are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the main evidence for the chapter's study of the city. So the capital's ruins are at Hampi.

stem: The ruins of Hampi were brought to scholarly light in 1800 largely through the efforts of __________, an engineer and antiquarian of the East India Company.
solution: The ruins of Hampi/Vijayanagara were 'discovered' and brought to scholarly attention in 1800 largely through the efforts of Colin Mackenzie — an engineer and antiquarian who became the first Surveyor General of India. He surveyed and documented the site and gathered local traditions and information about it. Later, the historian Robert Sewell wrote a well-known account ('A Forgotten Empire'), and epigraphists and archaeologists studied the inscriptions and monuments. So Hampi was brought to light by Colin Mackenzie.

stem: The greatest and most famous ruler of Vijayanagara, under whom the empire reached its zenith in the early 16th century, was __________.
solution: The most famous and powerful ruler of Vijayanagara was Krishnadeva Raya (r. 1509–1529) of the Tuluva dynasty, under whom the empire reached the height of its power, prosperity, and cultural achievement. He was a successful military commander (expanding and securing the empire), a great patron of art, architecture, and literature (himself a scholar and poet, author of the Amuktamalyada in Telugu), and he built temples and structures at the capital (including the Krishna temple and the Hazara Rama temple, and the gopurams). So the greatest ruler was Krishnadeva Raya.

stem: Vijayanagara was frequently at war with which rival powers to its north — a group of Deccan Muslim kingdoms?
options: The Bahmani Sultanate and its successor Deccan Sultanates
solution: Vijayanagara was frequently in conflict with the Bahmani Sultanate to its north (established in the Deccan in the 14th century), and later with the successor states — the Deccan Sultanates (like Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar, and Berar) — into which the Bahmani kingdom fragmented. These wars, often over fertile territory (like the Raichur doab between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers) and control of resources and trade, were a recurring feature of Deccan politics. So its northern rivals were the Bahmani Sultanate and the Deccan Sultanates.

stem: The catastrophic defeat that led to the sacking and abandonment of the capital city occurred in 1565 at the Battle of __________.
solution: In 1565, the forces of Vijayanagara were decisively defeated by a combined alliance of the Deccan Sultanates at the Battle of Talikota (also known as Rakshasi-Tangadi or Bannihatti). Following this catastrophic defeat, the magnificent capital city was captured, plundered, and largely destroyed and abandoned (the empire itself survived for some time under the Aravidu dynasty, shifting its centre southward, but the great city fell into ruin). So the decisive defeat was at the Battle of Talikota (1565).

stem: After 1565, the once-glorious capital was reduced to ruins and largely __________, which is why it survives mainly as an archaeological site.
options: Turned into a new Mughal capital
Rebuilt and still inhabited as a major city
solution: After the defeat at Talikota (1565), the capital city of Vijayanagara was plundered and largely destroyed, and it was subsequently abandoned/deserted — falling into ruin over the following centuries. This is why today it survives mainly as an extensive archaeological site (at Hampi), studied through its ruined temples, palaces, fortifications, and markets, along with inscriptions and travellers' accounts, rather than as a living city. So the capital was abandoned/deserted.

stem: Foreign travellers left valuable accounts of Vijayanagara. Which of the following visited and described the city?
options: The Portuguese Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz, and the Persian Abdur Razzaq (and the Italian Nicolo Conti)
Marco Polo and Vasco da Gama only
solution: Several foreign travellers visited Vijayanagara and left valuable descriptions of the city and empire: the Persian ambassador Abdur Razzaq (15th century), the Italian Nicolo Conti (15th century), and the Portuguese travellers Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (16th century), among others. Their accounts describe the city's size, wealth, fortifications, markets, court, and festivals, and are important sources (alongside archaeology and inscriptions) for reconstructing the city. So these travellers described Vijayanagara.

stem: Travellers were struck by the elaborate fortifications of Vijayanagara. A remarkable and unusual feature of the outer fortifications was that they enclosed not just the city but also __________.
options: Agricultural fields/farmland and their sources of water
solution: A remarkable and unusual feature of Vijayanagara's fortifications (noted by travellers like Abdur Razzaq) was that the massive outer walls enclosed not just the urban core but also large areas of AGRICULTURAL LAND (fields), along with their sources of water. This was a deliberate strategy: by enclosing farmland and water within the fortifications, the city could withstand long sieges by producing its own food and securing water, rather than being starved into surrender. So the fortifications enclosed agricultural fields and water sources.

stem: The elaborate systems built to bring and store water in this relatively arid region — including tanks, canals, and the large 'Kamalapuram tank' — show that the rulers invested heavily in __________.
solution: Because the Vijayanagara region was relatively arid, the rulers invested heavily in sophisticated systems of water harvesting, storage, and irrigation (hydraulic engineering): they built large tanks/reservoirs (like the one at Kamalapuram), canals to draw water from the Tungabhadra, embankments, and aqueducts to supply the city, its fields, and its people. This elaborate water management was essential to sustain the large population and the agriculture enclosed within the city. Archaeological remains of these hydraulic works survive. So they invested in water harvesting and irrigation engineering.

stem: The city of Vijayanagara can be broadly divided into distinct zones. The heavily fortified core containing the palaces, the king's audience halls, and administrative structures is called the __________.
solution: Archaeologists divide Vijayanagara into zones, including the 'Royal Centre' and the 'Sacred Centre'. The Royal Centre was the heavily fortified part of the city that contained the royal palaces, the king's audience hall and platforms (like the 'Mahanavami Dibba'), the administrative buildings, and structures associated with the court and the king's household (including the zenana). It was the political and ceremonial heart of the city. So the zone with palaces and administrative structures is the Royal Centre.

stem: The zone of the city dominated by temples, located mainly along the rocky riverbank of the Tungabhadra, is called the __________.
solution: The 'Sacred Centre' of Vijayanagara was the zone — situated mainly along the rocky stretch on the banks of the Tungabhadra river — that was dominated by TEMPLES. This area (associated with the sacred landscape linked to local legends, including those of the Ramayana and the goddess Pampadevi) contained major temple complexes such as the Virupaksha and the Vitthala temples. Temples were important not only religiously but also as centres of activity and power. So the temple-dominated zone is the Sacred Centre.

stem: The most important and ancient temple of the Sacred Centre, dedicated to a form of Shiva who was regarded as the guardian deity of the kingdom, was the __________.
solution: The Virupaksha temple was the most important and ancient temple of the Sacred Centre — dedicated to Virupaksha, a form of Shiva who was regarded as the guardian/tutelary deity of the Vijayanagara rulers. The temple predates the empire's foundation and was enlarged and embellished over time (its towering gopurams were added by rulers like Krishnadeva Raya). Kings associated their authority with this deity. So the guardian-deity temple is the Virupaksha temple. (Hampi is named after Pampa, associated with this sacred landscape.)

stem: The famous Vitthala temple at Vijayanagara is celebrated for its architectural features, including the iconic __________.
options: Stone chariot (ratha) and the musical/monolithic pillars
solution: The Vitthala temple (dedicated to Vitthala, a form of Vishnu) is one of the most spectacular monuments of Vijayanagara, celebrated for its exquisite architecture — including the iconic stone chariot (a shrine carved in the form of a temple-chariot/ratha) in its courtyard, and its remarkable pillared halls (mandapas) with intricately carved, slender 'musical' pillars (which are said to produce musical notes when struck). These reflect the high artistic achievement of Vijayanagara temple architecture. So the Vitthala temple is famous for its stone chariot and carved pillars.

stem: A distinctive architectural feature that developed prominently in Vijayanagara temple complexes was the __________ — the towering gateway.
solution: A distinctive and prominent feature of Vijayanagara temple architecture was the raya gopuram — the towering, monumental gateway (gopuram) built at the entrances of temple complexes, often on a grand scale by the kings (raya). These massive, richly carved gateway-towers dominated the temple's outer walls and skyline, and became characteristic of the Dravidian temple style as elaborated under Vijayanagara (and later Nayaka) patronage. Krishnadeva Raya, for instance, added grand gopurams. So the towering temple gateway is the (raya) gopuram.

stem: Other characteristic architectural features of Vijayanagara temples included the __________ — special pillared halls or pavilions used for various ceremonies and for the deity.
options: Mandapas (including the kalyana mandapa) and pillared corridors
solution: Vijayanagara temple complexes were characterised by elaborate mandapas (pillared halls/pavilions) and long pillared corridors. These included special halls such as the kalyana mandapa (used for the ceremonial 'marriage' of the deities), assembly and dance pavilions, and richly carved pillared halls where various rituals, festivals, and functions took place. The temples were thus large complexes with multiple structures, not just a single shrine. So characteristic features included the mandapas and pillared halls.

stem: In the Royal Centre stood a great platform, richly carved, associated with royal ceremonies and the celebration of a major festival. This platform is known as the __________.
solution: In the Royal Centre stood a massive, richly carved stone platform known as the Mahanavami Dibba (also referred to in connection with the 'audience hall'/great platform). It is associated with royal ceremonies, and especially with the celebration of the great festival of Mahanavami (Navaratri/Dussehra), during which the king witnessed grand ceremonies — processions, worship, sacrifices, music, dance, wrestling, and displays of the army, horses, and elephants — that reinforced royal power and authority. Its carvings depict such scenes. So the great platform is the Mahanavami Dibba.

stem: The great festival celebrated with much pomp at the capital, during which the king displayed his power and received homage, was the __________ (associated with Dussehra/Navaratri).
solution: The most important royal festival celebrated at Vijayanagara with great pomp and splendour was the Mahanavami festival (associated with Navaratri/Dussehra), lasting nine nights. During this festival, the king presided over elaborate ceremonies at the Mahanavami Dibba — including worship of the deity and the state horse and weapons, animal sacrifices, and grand displays of dancers, musicians, wrestlers, decorated horses and elephants, and the army — through which the ruler dramatised and reaffirmed his power, and received the homage of nobles and subordinate chiefs (nayakas). So the great royal festival was the Mahanavami.

stem: Some buildings in the Royal Centre, like the so-called 'Lotus Mahal' and the 'Elephant Stables', show a blending of architectural styles. This indicates that Vijayanagara architecture:
options: Was purely and rigidly of one single style
Combined indigenous (Hindu/temple) styles with Indo-Islamic (Deccan Sultanate) architectural influences, especially in secular/courtly buildings
solution: Buildings in the Royal Centre such as the 'Lotus Mahal' (a pavilion, possibly a council chamber) and the 'Elephant Stables' display features — like arches, domes, and vaults — that reflect Indo-Islamic (Deccan Sultanate) architectural influences, blended with indigenous elements. This shows that Vijayanagara architecture, especially in its SECULAR/courtly buildings, combined indigenous (Hindu/temple) traditions with Indo-Islamic influences absorbed from interaction with the neighbouring Sultanates — an example of cultural synthesis. (The temples, by contrast, largely continued the Dravidian tradition.) So Vijayanagara architecture blended indigenous and Indo-Islamic styles. This is an important point.

stem: The 'Elephant Stables' and 'Lotus Mahal' are among the few surviving buildings of the __________, since most secular royal structures were destroyed.
solution: The 'Elephant Stables' (a row of grand domed chambers for the royal elephants) and the 'Lotus Mahal' are among the few relatively well-preserved buildings of the ROYAL/courtly area of Vijayanagara. Most of the secular royal structures (palaces, halls, and residential buildings, which were often built partly of perishable materials on stone/masonry bases, and were deliberately destroyed after 1565) have not survived well, so these surviving structures are especially valuable for understanding the courtly architecture. So they belong to the royal/courtly palace area.

stem: The powerful military commanders/chiefs of the Vijayanagara Empire, who were assigned territories in return for maintaining troops and paying tribute, were called __________.
solution: The Vijayanagara military and administrative system relied heavily on the nayakas — military commanders/chiefs who were often assigned control over territories. Under the amara-nayaka system, a nayaka was granted the right to collect revenue and control a territory (an 'amaram') in return for maintaining a specified body of troops (horses, elephants, and soldiers) for the king, paying tribute/dues, and providing military service. This system (with some resemblance to the iqta and later Mughal arrangements) was central to how the empire was governed and defended. So the military chiefs were the nayakas.

stem: Under the amara-nayaka system, a key obligation of the nayakas to the king was to __________.
options: Maintain military contingents (troops, horses, elephants) for the king and remit tribute/revenue, while providing military service
solution: Under the amara-nayaka system, the nayakas (military chiefs) were assigned territories from which they collected revenue; in return, their key obligations to the king were to maintain a stipulated number of military contingents — troops, horses, and elephants — for the empire's use, to render military service when required, and to remit a portion of the revenue as tribute/dues to the central treasury. Some nayakas also sent horses and elephants and paid homage at the capital during festivals (like Mahanavami). Over time, some nayakas grew powerful and, after the empire's decline, became independent rulers. So their obligation was to maintain troops and remit tribute while serving militarily.

stem: The prosperity of Vijayanagara depended greatly on trade. Which commodity, important for the cavalry and warfare, was a major and prized import through its ports?
options: Horses (especially from Arabia and Central Asia)
solution: A major and highly prized import of Vijayanagara was HORSES (especially fine warhorses from Arabia and Central Asia), which were essential for the cavalry and hence for military power. Because good warhorses were not bred well locally, the empire imported large numbers through its ports (on the west coast), and control of this horse trade was strategically and economically important (the Portuguese, controlling coastal trade, became significant suppliers). So horses were a major prized import. Vijayanagara also traded in spices, textiles, precious stones, and other goods, and its markets impressed foreign travellers.

stem: Travellers described the bazaars of Vijayanagara as full of precious goods. This, along with the city's size and splendour, indicates that Vijayanagara was:
options: A large, wealthy, and cosmopolitan commercial and imperial city, deeply engaged in long-distance and regional trade
Purely a military fort with no economy
solution: Foreign travellers (like Abdur Razzaq and Paes) described Vijayanagara as an enormous, splendid, and immensely wealthy city, with bustling bazaars full of precious goods — gold, gems, pearls, fine textiles, and spices — and a large, diverse population. This indicates that Vijayanagara was a large, prosperous, and cosmopolitan commercial and imperial city, deeply engaged in both long-distance/overseas trade (through its ports) and regional/internal trade, and a centre of consumption, craft production, and exchange. So it was a wealthy, cosmopolitan commercial and imperial city.

stem: The sources historians use to reconstruct Vijayanagara include archaeological remains, inscriptions, and __________.
options: Foreign travellers' accounts and contemporary literary works (in Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, Tamil)
solution: Historians reconstruct Vijayanagara from a combination of sources: ARCHAEOLOGICAL remains (the ruins at Hampi — temples, palaces, fortifications, water systems, markets, sculptures); INSCRIPTIONS (epigraphic records on stone and copper, giving details of grants, administration, and events); the accounts of FOREIGN TRAVELLERS (Abdur Razzaq, Nicolo Conti, Paes, Nuniz, etc.); and contemporary LITERARY works composed in Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada, and Tamil (the empire was a great patron of literature). Combining these varied sources gives a fuller picture. So the sources include travellers' accounts and literary works, alongside archaeology and inscriptions.

stem: Vijayanagara rulers were great patrons of __________, and the court supported works in Sanskrit and the southern languages (Telugu, Kannada, Tamil).
solution: The Vijayanagara rulers (especially Krishnadeva Raya) were great patrons of literature, the arts, learning, temple-building, and culture. The court supported the composition of literary works in Sanskrit and in the major southern languages — Telugu, Kannada, and Tamil — and this era is regarded as a golden age for Telugu literature in particular (Krishnadeva Raya's own Telugu work, the Amuktamalyada, and the poets of his court, the 'ashtadiggajas'). Temples and the arts flourished under their patronage. So the rulers were great patrons of literature and the arts.

stem: The layout of the city — with the Royal Centre, the Sacred Centre, temples associated with the sacred landscape, and the integration of a local goddess (Pampadevi) and Ramayana associations — shows that the rulers sought to link their power with __________.
options: Religious and mythical sanction (associating kingship with the sacred landscape and deities)
solution: The city's layout and its sacred geography reveal that the Vijayanagara rulers sought to link their political power with RELIGIOUS and MYTHICAL sanction. The Sacred Centre and its temples (especially the Virupaksha temple of the guardian deity Shiva-Virupaksha, and the associations with the goddess Pampadevi and with episodes of the Ramayana believed to have occurred in this landscape) tied the kingship and the city to divine and mythic authority. Royal ceremonies (like Mahanavami) and temple patronage further sacralised the ruler's power. So the rulers linked their power with religious/mythical sanction. This is an important interpretive point.

stem: Which statement about the Vijayanagara ruler's relationship with temples is correct?
options: Rulers actively patronised temples (building and endowing them), associated themselves with important deities, and used temple patronage as a means of asserting and legitimising royal authority
Temples were forbidden in the empire
solution: Vijayanagara rulers actively patronised temples: they built new temples and gopurams, made lavish grants and endowments to temples, and closely associated themselves with important deities (like Virupaksha, the guardian deity, and Vitthala). Temple patronage was not merely religious devotion — it was also an important means of asserting and LEGITIMISING royal authority: by supporting temples and linking themselves to the gods, kings enhanced their prestige, integrated the sacred landscape into their rule, and bound temple institutions (which were also economic and social centres) to the state. So rulers used temple patronage to assert and legitimise their authority. This is a key theme.

stem: Assertion (A): The fortifications of Vijayanagara enclosed agricultural fields and water sources within the city walls. Reason (R): This design enabled the city to withstand prolonged sieges by ensuring an internal supply of food and water. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that Vijayanagara's massive fortifications enclosed not just the built-up city but also agricultural fields and their water sources. And the reason is (R) that this deliberate design allowed the city to withstand prolonged sieges: with farmland and water secured inside the walls, the defenders could produce food and access water even during a long blockade, rather than being starved into surrender. So the siege-resistance rationale directly explains why fields and water were enclosed (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The 'Lotus Mahal' and 'Elephant Stables' at Vijayanagara show Indo-Islamic architectural features like arches and domes. Reason (R): Vijayanagara was in close and constant contact (through war, diplomacy, and trade) with the neighbouring Deccan Sultanates, leading to cultural and architectural exchange. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that courtly buildings like the Lotus Mahal and Elephant Stables incorporate Indo-Islamic features such as arches, domes, and vaults. And the reason is (R) that Vijayanagara was in close and continuous contact with the neighbouring Deccan Sultanates — through recurrent warfare, diplomacy, and trade — which led to significant cultural and architectural exchange and the absorption of Indo-Islamic styles, especially in secular/courtly architecture. This ongoing interaction directly explains the presence of such features (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The interpretation of a large building as the 'Elephant Stables' or another as the 'Lotus Mahal' or 'zenana' by early scholars illustrates that:
options: Archaeological interpretation is always certain and final
The functions/names of ruined secular buildings are often uncertain and based on inference — these are modern labels, and interpretations can be debated or revised
The buildings were labelled by the Vijayanagara kings themselves
solution: Names like 'Elephant Stables', 'Lotus Mahal', and 'zenana enclosure' are MODERN labels given by later scholars/observers, based on inference about the buildings' probable functions — not names from the Vijayanagara period itself. Because the secular buildings are ruined and lack clear labels, their original functions are often uncertain and their identifications can be debated and revised as scholarship advances. This illustrates the interpretive and provisional nature of archaeological reconstruction — a key methodological point of the chapter (how historians 'read' ruins). So option 2 is correct.

stem: The empire's reliance on nayakas and the amara-nayaka system, while militarily useful, carried a long-term risk because:
options: Powerful nayakas could become semi-independent and, especially as central authority weakened (after 1565), assert autonomy or found their own states
The system had no effect on politics
solution: While the amara-nayaka system was militarily and administratively useful (providing troops and local governance), it carried a long-term structural risk: the nayakas, controlling territory, revenue, and their own military contingents, could grow powerful and semi-independent. As long as the centre was strong, they were kept in check, but when central authority weakened — especially after the catastrophic defeat at Talikota (1565) and the empire's decline — several powerful nayakas asserted their autonomy and eventually founded their own independent states (the Nayaka kingdoms, e.g., of Madurai, Tanjavur, and Gingee). So the risk was that nayakas could become independent as central power waned. This is an important analytical point.

stem: The Vijayanagara Empire was ruled successively by four dynasties. Which of the following gives them in the correct order?
solution: The Vijayanagara Empire was ruled by four successive dynasties: the Sangama (the founding dynasty of Harihara and Bukka), followed by the Saluva, then the Tuluva (to which the greatest ruler, Krishnadeva Raya, belonged), and finally the Aravidu (under whom the empire survived, in reduced form, after the disaster of 1565). So the correct order is Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu. Knowing this dynastic sequence is prelims-relevant.

stem: The name 'Hampi' is derived from __________, the local name associated with the goddess and the sacred landscape of the site.
solution: The name 'Hampi' is derived from Pampa (Pampadevi) — the local goddess (identified with the river/landscape) associated with the sacred geography of the site. The Tungabhadra river itself was linked with Pampa, and the Virupaksha temple is connected with the Pampa-Virupaksha tradition. This local sacred association was woven into the identity and legitimacy of the city and its rulers. So 'Hampi' comes from Pampadevi.

stem: The Portuguese established a strong presence on the west coast during the Vijayanagara period and became important in the region's trade, especially in the supply of __________ to Vijayanagara.
solution: During the Vijayanagara period (16th century), the Portuguese established themselves on the west coast (e.g., at Goa) and became important players in coastal and maritime trade. In particular, they became significant suppliers of warhorses (imported from Arabia and elsewhere) to Vijayanagara — a strategically vital commodity for the empire's cavalry. This trade relationship was economically and militarily important and also gave the Portuguese leverage in Deccan politics. So the Portuguese were especially important in supplying horses.

stem: The Persian ambassador who visited Vijayanagara in the 15th century and left a detailed and admiring description of the city (including its seven lines of fortifications and bustling bazaars) was __________.
solution: Abdur Razzaq was a Persian ambassador (from the court of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh of Herat) who visited Vijayanagara in the 15th century (during the reign of Deva Raya II). He left a detailed and admiring account of the city — describing its multiple concentric lines of fortifications, the space between the walls (including cultivated fields), the prosperous bazaars, the palace, and the wealth and grandeur of the capital. His account is an important source. So the Persian ambassador was Abdur Razzaq.

stem: Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz, who left valuable accounts of Vijayanagara, were travellers of which nationality?
solution: Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz were Portuguese travellers/chroniclers who visited Vijayanagara in the 16th century and left valuable accounts. Paes (who visited during the reign of Krishnadeva Raya) described the city, its people, the king, the court, and festivals like the Mahanavami in vivid detail; Nuniz wrote about the empire's history and administration. Their accounts (reflecting the Portuguese presence on the coast) are important sources. So Paes and Nuniz were Portuguese.

stem: The extensive ruins of Vijayanagara at Hampi have been recognised for their global importance by being designated a __________.
solution: The Group of Monuments at Hampi (the ruins of Vijayanagara) has been recognised for its outstanding universal value and designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This status reflects the exceptional historical, architectural, and cultural importance of the extensive ruins — temples, palaces, markets, fortifications, and water systems — and has aided their preservation and study. So Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

stem: The historian who wrote the well-known book 'A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagar)', drawing on Portuguese accounts, was __________.
solution: Robert Sewell, a British historian, wrote the well-known book 'A Forgotten Empire (Vijayanagar)' (published in 1900), which drew heavily on the accounts of Portuguese travellers (like Paes and Nuniz) along with other sources to reconstruct the history of the empire. His work helped popularise the study of Vijayanagara. (Colin Mackenzie had earlier surveyed the ruins in 1800.) So the author of 'A Forgotten Empire' was Robert Sewell.

stem: The 'ashtadiggajas' ('eight elephants'/eight great poets) were associated with the court of which Vijayanagara ruler, reflecting the flourishing of Telugu literature?
solution: The 'ashtadiggajas' (literally the 'eight elephants [guarding the directions]') were the eight great poets said to have adorned the court of Krishnadeva Raya — a sign of the golden age of Telugu literature under his patronage. Krishnadeva Raya was himself a scholar and poet (author of the Telugu work Amuktamalyada). His court's literary brilliance reflects the strong cultural patronage of the Vijayanagara rulers. So the ashtadiggajas were associated with Krishnadeva Raya.

stem: Krishnadeva Raya composed a famous work in Telugu on statecraft and devotion titled __________.
solution: Krishnadeva Raya composed the Amuktamalyada, a celebrated work in Telugu (also containing reflections on kingship, statecraft, and administration, alongside its devotional/narrative content relating to the Alvar saint Andal/Goda). This reflects both his personal learning and the flourishing of Telugu literature under his patronage. So his famous Telugu work is the Amuktamalyada. (The Ain-i-Akbari is Abul Fazl's; the Rajatarangini is Kalhana's; the Arthashastra is Kautilya's.)

stem: The recurring wars between Vijayanagara and the Deccan Sultanates were often fought over the fertile, contested region between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers, known as the __________.
solution: A frequent bone of contention between Vijayanagara and the Bahmani/Deccan Sultanates was the Raichur doab — the fertile and strategically important tract of land lying between the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers. Control of this rich agricultural region (and its resources and revenue) was fought over repeatedly. So the contested region was the Raichur doab. (A 'doab' is the land between two rivers.)

stem: The alliance of Deccan Sultanates that defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565) is significant because it shows that:
options: Despite their frequent mutual rivalries, the Deccan Sultanates could unite against a common rival (Vijayanagara) when it suited them
solution: The Battle of Talikota (1565) was won by a COMBINED alliance of several Deccan Sultanates (such as Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, and Bidar) acting together against Vijayanagara. This is significant because these Sultanates were normally rivals who fought among themselves, yet they could set aside their mutual conflicts and unite when it served their common interest — here, to crush the powerful Vijayanagara Empire. It illustrates the shifting, pragmatic alliances of Deccan politics (which cut across any simple 'Hindu vs Muslim' framing, since alliances were fluid and interest-based). So the alliance shows the Sultanates could unite against a common rival. This is an important nuance.

stem: Political alliances in the Deccan (between Vijayanagara and the Sultanates) were often based on __________ rather than purely on religion.
options: Strategic and political interests (shifting, pragmatic alliances that sometimes crossed 'Hindu-Muslim' lines)
solution: Historians emphasise that the political alliances and conflicts in the Deccan — between Vijayanagara and the various Sultanates — were driven largely by strategic and political interests (territory, resources, power, and rivalry) rather than purely by religion. Alliances shifted pragmatically: Vijayanagara sometimes allied with one Sultanate against another, and the Sultanates fought among themselves as often as against Vijayanagara. Thus the politics cannot be reduced to a simple, constant 'Hindu vs Muslim' conflict; interest and expediency shaped alliances that could cross religious lines. So alliances were based on strategic/political interests. This is an important corrective point.

stem: The extensive market streets (bazaars) found near temples like the Virupaksha and Vitthala temples suggest that in Vijayanagara, temples were also __________.
options: Important centres of economic activity and social life (with associated markets, and roles in the economy), not just places of worship
solution: The presence of long market streets/bazaars associated with major temples (such as those near the Virupaksha and Vitthala temples) indicates that temples in Vijayanagara were much more than places of worship — they were important centres of ECONOMIC and SOCIAL activity. Temples were hubs of trade and markets, owned land and resources, employed many people, hosted festivals and gatherings, and functioned as significant institutions in the urban economy and community life. This integration of temple, market, and community is an important feature of the city. So temples were also economic and social centres.

stem: Archaeological study of Vijayanagara has involved carefully mapping the site, recording surface finds, and analysing structures. This shows that reconstructing the city relies heavily on __________.
options: Systematic archaeological survey and documentation, combined with inscriptions and textual/travellers' accounts
solution: Reconstructing Vijayanagara has relied heavily on systematic ARCHAEOLOGICAL work — carefully surveying and mapping the extensive site, recording and analysing surface finds, structures, sculptures, and the layout of zones and water systems — combined with the evidence of INSCRIPTIONS and TEXTUAL sources (contemporary literature and the accounts of foreign travellers). Integrating these different kinds of evidence allows historians to interpret the ruins and understand how the city was organised and functioned. So reconstruction relies on systematic archaeological survey plus inscriptions and texts. This methodological emphasis is central to the chapter.

stem: The 'Hazara Rama temple', located within the Royal Centre and decorated with sculpted panels depicting scenes from the Ramayana, is thought to have been __________.
options: A private/royal chapel of the king (associated with the royal household)
solution: The Hazara Rama temple, situated within the Royal Centre, is generally thought to have served as a private or royal chapel — a temple associated with the king and the royal household (rather than a large public temple). It is notable for its finely sculpted panels depicting scenes from the Ramayana (on its walls), reflecting the close association of the rulers with the Rama tradition and the sacred narratives woven into the city. So it is interpreted as the king's private/royal temple.

stem: Which of the following best summarises WHY the study of the ruined city of Vijayanagara is valuable to historians?
options: The physical remains — combined with inscriptions and travellers' accounts — reveal how a great pre-modern empire organised urban space, water, defence, religion, ceremony, administration, and economy, and how power was expressed and legitimised
It is valuable only for tourism
solution: The study of Vijayanagara's ruins is valuable because the physical remains of the city — its fortifications, hydraulic systems, zoning (Royal and Sacred Centres), palaces and ceremonial platforms, temples and markets — combined with inscriptions and the accounts of foreign travellers, allow historians to understand a great deal about how a major pre-modern empire actually organised urban space, water supply, defence, religious life, royal ceremony, administration (the nayaka system), and economy/trade — and how the rulers expressed, dramatised, and legitimised their power. In other words, the capital is a window onto the whole society, politics, and culture of the empire. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara' is that:
options: Vijayanagara was an insignificant village with no history

Vijayanagara (founded in 1336, with its capital at present-day Hampi) was a powerful, wealthy, and splendid South Indian empire — reaching its height under Krishnadeva Raya — whose magnificent capital, reconstructed from ruins, inscriptions, and travellers' accounts, reveals through its fortifications, water systems, Royal and Sacred Centres, temples (Virupaksha, Vitthala), gopurams, courtly buildings blending Hindu and Indo-Islamic styles, festivals (Mahanavami), the nayaka system, and thriving trade, how the rulers organised, sustained, and legitimised their power — until its destruction after the Battle of Talikota in 1565
The city was built by the Mughals
Vijayanagara had no temples or trade
solution: The chapter's overall message is that Vijayanagara — founded around 1336 (by Harihara and Bukka), with its great capital at present-day Hampi on the Tungabhadra — was one of the most powerful, prosperous, and culturally splendid empires of South India, reaching its zenith under Krishnadeva Raya in the early 16th century. Studying its capital (reconstructed by historians from the archaeological ruins, inscriptions, and the accounts of foreign travellers like Abdur Razzaq, Paes, and Nuniz) reveals a great deal about how power was organised, sustained, and legitimised: through massive fortifications enclosing fields and water (for siege resistance) and elaborate hydraulic/irrigation systems; through the layout of the city into a Royal Centre (with palaces, the Mahanavami Dibba, and courtly buildings like the Lotus Mahal and Elephant Stables that blend Hindu and Indo-Islamic styles) and a Sacred Centre (with grand temples such as Virupaksha — the guardian deity — and Vitthala, with their gopurams, mandapas, and the stone chariot); through royal ceremonies and festivals like the Mahanavami that dramatised royal power; through the amara-nayaka military-administrative system; and through flourishing trade (importing prized warhorses) and rich literary/artistic patronage. This magnificent city and empire were shattered after the decisive defeat by the combined Deccan Sultanates at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, after which the capital was plundered and abandoned. So the overall message is option 2.
